questions.q: Why define a custom exception like RateLimitError instead of making callers check resp.status_code themselves?
options: Custom exceptions run faster than status code checks
It gives callers a clean, named error to catch instead of inspecting raw HTTP codes everywhere
requests cannot return status codes
It's required by the Messages API
questions.explain: A custom exception centralizes the meaning of 'this failed in a retryable way' into one clearly named type callers can catch.

questions.q: In the retry loop example, which status codes trigger a retry with backoff?
options: 400 and 401 only
404 only
429 and any 5xx status
Every status code, including 200
questions.explain: 429 (rate limit) and 5xx (server-side) are the transient failures worth retrying, matching Lesson 14's guidance.

questions.q: What happens in the example loop when a non-retryable error (like a 400) comes back?
options: resp.raise_for_status() raises immediately — no retry happens
It's silently ignored and None is returned
It retries exactly like a 429 would
The program exits without an exception
questions.explain: Only 429/5xx trigger the retry branch; anything else falls through to raise_for_status(), which raises right away.

questions.q: Why does this lesson put the retry logic inside the client class's send_message method, rather than in each calling script?
options: Python classes execute retries automatically with no code needed
So every caller gets consistent resilience without duplicating (and potentially mis-copying) the same loop everywhere
Because retry logic cannot exist outside a class
It has no real benefit, it's just a style preference
questions.explain: Centralizing retry logic on the class means one correct implementation benefits every caller, instead of twenty copy-pasted (and possibly buggy) versions.

questions.q: What does raise RateLimitError("Retries exhausted") communicate that returning None would not?
options: Nothing — they're functionally identical
It explicitly signals failure, forcing the caller to handle it instead of silently treating a failure as a valid empty result
It automatically retries one more time
It converts the error into a successful response
questions.explain: Raising an exception makes a failure impossible to silently ignore; returning None could be mistaken for a legitimate (if empty) result.
